docs.title: Define your tests
docs.text: Test definitions validate built images using container-structure-test. They are rendered during ch generate and executed by ch test.

docs.title: File location
docs.text:
Place a test.yml or test.yml.gotpl file alongside the Dockerfile in the image directory. The .gotpl extension is optional — use it when you need Go template variables (versions, build args). Plain test.yml files are copied as-is.

images/my-image/
├── image.yml
├── Dockerfile
└── test.yml.gotpl

Variants can have their own test definitions:

images/my-image/
├── image.yml
├── Dockerfile
├── test.yml.gotpl
└── slim/
    ├── Dockerfile
    └── test.yml.gotpl

When both an image-level and variant-level test file exist, both are collected and executed.

docs.title: Template context
docs.text:
The template receives a TemplateContext with the following fields:

Field Type Description Versions map Version values resolved from image, tag, and variant definitions BuildArgs map Build arguments resolved from image, tag, and variant definitions ImageName string The name of the image

Values follow a merge hierarchy: image defaults -> tag overrides -> variant overrides.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text: Test files use the container-structure-test schema version 2.0.0. The following test types are supported:

docs.title: Command tests
docs.text:
Run a command inside the container and check the output:

schemaVersion: 2.0.0
commandTests:
  - name: "Python version"
    command: "python"
    args: ["--version"]
    expectedOutput: ["Python {{ .Versions.python }}"]

docs.title: File existence tests
docs.text:
Check that files exist (or don't) with expected permissions:

schemaVersion: 2.0.0
fileExistenceTests:
  - name: "Binary exists"
    path: "/usr/local/bin/my-app"
    shouldExist: true
    permissions: "-rwxr-xr-x"

docs.title: File content tests
docs.text:
Check the contents of files in the image:

schemaVersion: 2.0.0
fileContentTests:
  - name: "Config contains production"
    path: "/etc/my-app/config.yml"
    expectedContents: ["production"]

docs.title: Metadata tests
docs.text:
Validate image metadata like labels and environment variables:

schemaVersion: 2.0.0
metadataTest:
  labels:
    - key: "app"
      value: "{{ .ImageName }}"
  envVars:
    - key: "APP_VERSION"
      value: "{{ .Versions.app }}"

docs.title: Template functions
docs.text:
Templates have access to all Sprig functions plus:

Function Description resolve_base(name, tag) Produces an internal image reference for inter-image dependencies

docs.title: Version check with Go template variable
docs.text:
schemaVersion: 2.0.0
commandTests:
  - name: "go-version"
    command: "go"
    args: ["version"]
    expectedOutput: ["go{{ .Versions.go }}"]
metadataTest:
  labels:
    - key: "app"
      value: "{{ .ImageName }}"

docs.title: Rootfs file validation
docs.text:
schemaVersion: 2.0.0
commandTests:
  - name: "python-version"
    command: "python"
    args: ["--version"]
    expectedOutput: ["Python {{ .Versions.python }}"]

fileExistenceTests:
  - name: "rootfs-python-info-exists"
    path: "/etc/python-info"
    shouldExist: true

fileContentTests:
  - name: "rootfs-python-info-has-version-level-content"
    path: "/etc/python-info"
    expectedContents: ["level=version"]

docs.title: Variant-specific test
docs.text:
schemaVersion: 2.0.0
commandTests:
  - name: "node-version"
    command: "node"
    args: ["--version"]
    expectedOutput: ["{{ .Versions.nodejs }}"]

docs.title: Rendered output
docs.text:
During ch generate, test templates are rendered to dist/<image>/<tag>/tests/:

dist/my-image/latest/tests/
├── image.yml       # from image-level test.yml.gotpl
└── variant.yml     # from variant-level test.yml.gotpl (if present)

These rendered files are consumed by ch test using container-structure-test.

For more on running tests, see Container Structure Tests.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: ContainerHive welcomes contributions — bug reports, discussions, fixes, and new features. The contribution guidelines in the repository describe the pull request flow, required quality standards, and the AI-generated contributions policy.

docs.title: Maintainers wanted
docs.text:
ContainerHive currently has a single maintainer: Timo Reymann. To keep reviews, releases, and urgent fixes going even when that one person is unavailable, additional maintainers are welcome.

You do not take over the project: responsibilities and expectations are discussed before anything is assigned to you. Shared ownership is the goal, not a handover.

If you are interested, reach out to oss@timo-reymann.de to talk details.

docs.title: What maintainers work on
docs.text:
• Reviewing and merging pull requests
  • Cutting releases
  • Triage of issues and pull requests
  • Urgent fixes, including when the release process runs without the original maintainer

docs.title: Set up local development
docs.text:
If you want to work on ContainerHive you can do so, easily.

Before starting to develop make sure you have read the Contribution Guidelines.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Make sure to install the following tools:

  • Go
  • GNU make
  • Docker
  • pre-commit

docs.title: Run
docs.text: go run ./cmd/ch/ -h

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
Run tests and show the coverage report in your default browser.

make test-coverage-report

Run specific package tests:

go test ./internal/dependency/...

Skip integration tests:

go test -short ./...

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Build binaries for all platforms.

make build

docs.title: Generate embedded resources
docs.text:
Required before building.

make generate

docs.title: Preview documentation
docs.text:
Preview the properdocs documentation locally with hot-reload for changes.

pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
properdocs serve

docs.title: AI usage
docs.text: This project uses AI tooling (Claude Code and Mistral AI models) to assist with development. All AI-generated or AI-assisted changes are human-reviewed and applied responsibly — this is not AI slop. Contributors are expected to uphold the same standard: AI tools are welcome, but every change must be understood, reviewed, and owned by the person submitting it.

docs.title: Snapshot builds and internal releases
docs.text:
hack/release-snapshot.sh builds a ContainerHive image from any git ref or pull request and pushes it to a registry of your choice. The Go binaries compile inside a Docker container, the build artifacts land on the host, and the image is built for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.

This is the fastest way to consume a fix from a pull request, and it works without any maintainer involvement — for example when a critical fix has to ship while the maintainer is unavailable.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• bash 3 or newer
  • git
  • docker with a reachable daemon
  • docker buildx (the script creates its own builder if none exists)
  • Registry credentials are handled by the caller: docker login, a credential helper, or a company authorization tool. The script performs no authorization checks itself.

On a plain Linux host, cross-arch emulation may be missing. If the arm64 build fails, run:

docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install all

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
./hack/release-snapshot.sh [--ref <git-ref>] [--pr <id>] \
    --target <registry.tld/image> [--tag <tag>] [--no-push]
Flag Meaning --pr <id> Build from refs/pull/<id>/head. Fetched into a detached worktree, so your checkout stays clean. --ref <git-ref> Build from any git ref: HEAD, a commit hash, a branch, or a tag. --target Target image without tag, for example registry.tld/containerhive. --tag Tag for the image. Defaults to pr-<id> for --pr and rev-<short-sha> otherwise. Sanitized to a docker-safe tag. --no-push Build a single-arch image for the host platform and load it into the local Docker store.

With no flags at all the script asks interactively: source, target, and tag — using bash-tui-toolkit.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Publish a pull request build for testing:

./hack/release-snapshot.sh --pr 42 --target registry.tld/containerhive
# -> registry.tld/containerhive:pr-42 (+ :sha-<short>) for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64

Build the current HEAD without pushing:

./hack/release-snapshot.sh --no-push --target registry.tld/containerhive

Release an urgent internal fix with an explicit version:

./hack/release-snapshot.sh --pr 42 --target registry.tld/internal/containerhive --tag 1.4.2-internal.3

docs.title: Where the artifacts go
docs.text: Build artifacts land in dist-snapshot/<tag>/ (configure the parent folder with DIST_SNAPSHOT_DIR). The folder holds the dist/*.tar.zst archives plus the assembled Docker build context. The path is gitignored.

docs.title: Urgent fix flow (maintainer unavailable)
docs.text:
1. A contributor opens the hotfix pull request.
  2. Someone runs ./hack/release-snapshot.sh --pr <id> --target <your-registry/image>.
  3. Test the resulting pr-<id> image in your pipeline.
  4. The fix ships from the pull request ref; upstream merges follow later through the normal review flow.

No write or maintainer access is needed at any step.

docs.title: Build Process Overview
docs.text: ContainerHive builds container images through a pipeline of five steps:

docs.title: Pipeline Steps
docs.text:
1. Discovery (ch generate) - Find and validate hive.yml and image definitions.
  2. Dependency Resolution - Build the dependency graph from FROM __hive__/<image>:<tag> references and explicit depends_on entries.
  3. Preparation (ch generate) - Apply templates and render build contexts to dist/.
  4. Execution (ch build) - Build images with BuildKit in dependency order.
  5. Post-Processing (ch test, ch sbom, ch finalize) - Run tests, generate SBOMs, create multi-arch manifests and alias tags.

docs.title: Execution model
docs.text:
• A single ch build run builds images one after another in dependency order, so a parent always exists before its children.
  • To build in parallel, split the work across jobs. The generated CI pipeline has one stage per dependency depth, and sharding spreads the images of a stage across parallel jobs. See How dependency resolution works.
  • Within one ch build run, parent images are passed to children as OCI layout named contexts, so no registry push is needed between steps. With sharding, a parent built by another shard is not in the local layout: it resolves via the registry and must already be pushed there.

docs.title: Other behavior
docs.text:
• Templates are processed with Go templates, see Write your Dockerfiles.
  • Secrets are passed through BuildKit secret mounts, see Secrets and versions.
  • A failed build stops the run with a non-zero exit code. Nothing is pushed for images that were not built.

docs.title: How dependency resolution works
docs.text: ContainerHive builds images in the correct order by resolving dependencies between them.

docs.title: How dependencies are discovered
docs.text:
Dependencies are resolved from two sources:

  1. Explicit declaration: The depends_on field in image.yml lists images this image depends on.
  2. Automatic detection: ContainerHive scans FROM statements in Dockerfiles to detect references to other images in the project.

Both sources are combined to build a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that determines the build order.

docs.title: Build order
docs.text:
Images are grouped into layers based on their dependency depth:

  1. Images with no dependencies are built first (depth 0).
  2. Images depending only on depth-0 images are built next (depth 1).
  3. This continues until all images are built.

Images at the same depth can be built in parallel.

docs.title: Inter-image dependencies
docs.text: When an image depends on another image in the project, ContainerHive uses OCI layout named contexts to pass the built image as a build context. This avoids needing to push intermediate images to a remote registry.

docs.title: CI pipeline generation
docs.text: The dependency graph is also used to generate CI pipelines. Each depth level becomes a stage in the generated pipeline, allowing the CI system to parallelize builds within each stage.

docs.title: How SBOM generation works
docs.text: ContainerHive generates Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) for built images using Syft.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
Syft is integrated as a Go library rather than invoked as an external tool. This means:

  • No additional runtime dependencies or Docker-in-Docker setup needed.
  • Works in air-gapped and network-restricted environments.
  • Operates directly on local OCI tar files produced during the build.

docs.title: Output format
docs.text: SBOMs are generated in CycloneDX JSON format. Each image produces a cyclonedx.json file in its output directory.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
ch sbom

The sbom command must run after build, as it operates on the built image artifacts.

docs.title: Use build IDs for merge requests
docs.text: The --build-id flag appends a unique identifier to all image tags, allowing multiple builds to coexist in the same registry without overwriting each other. This is essential for merge request (MR) / pull request (PR) workflows where you want to build, test, and preview images before merging.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When you pass --build-id, all tags get a -build.<id> suffix:

Tag Build ID Result 1.0.0 mr-42 1.0.0-build.mr-42 1.0.0 build-1234 1.0.0-build.build-1234

The -build. infix keeps suffixed tags unambiguous — 26.06-build.22 cannot be mistaken for a patch release 26.06.22.

This applies to:

  • Platform-specific push tags (e.g. 1.0.0.linux-amd64-build.mr-42)
  • Multi-arch manifest tags created by finalize (e.g. 1.0.0-build.mr-42)
  • Semantic version aliases created by finalize (e.g. 1-build.mr-42, 1.0-build.mr-42)

docs.title: 1. Build with a build ID
docs.text:
Use the MR/PR number or CI job ID as the build ID:

# GitLab CI
ch --build-id "mr-${CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID}" build

# GitHub Actions
ch --build-id "pr-${GITHUB_EVENT_NUMBER}" build

docs.title: 2. Finalize with the same build ID
docs.text:
ch --build-id "mr-${CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID}" finalize

This creates manifests like my-image:1.0.0-build.mr-42 and aliases like my-image:1-build.mr-42.

docs.title: 3. Test with the same build ID
docs.text: ch --build-id "mr-${CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID}" test

docs.title: 4. Merge and build without build ID
docs.text:
On the main branch, build without --build-id to produce the final tags:

ch build
ch finalize

This creates the clean my-image:1.0.0 tag and aliases my-image:1.0, my-image:1.

docs.title: Why use build IDs
docs.text:
Without build IDs, concurrent MR builds would overwrite each other's tags in the registry. Build IDs solve this by namespacing tags per MR:

  • MR 42 pushes 1.0.0-build.mr-42 — safe to test and preview
  • MR 43 pushes 1.0.0-build.mr-43 — doesn't conflict with MR 42
  • Main branch pushes 1.0.0 — the final, clean tag after merge

docs.title: Flag placement
docs.text:
--build-id is a global flag, placed before the subcommand:

ch --build-id "mr-42" build
ch --build-id "mr-42" finalize
ch --build-id "mr-42" test
ch --build-id "mr-42" sbom

Use the same build ID across all commands in a single pipeline run to keep tags consistent.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Build-ID suffixed images accumulate in the registry on every MR/PR run — even if the MR is never merged. Set up a retention policy to automatically clean up these snapshots after a few days. Tags containing -build. are safe to delete because production tags (e.g. 1.0.0) never carry the -build. infix.

See Clean up registry images with retention policies for per-provider setup instructions.

docs.title: Set up build caching
docs.text: ContainerHive supports build layer caching through BuildKit, using either S3-compatible storage or a container registry as the cache backend. Caching is configured in hive.yml and applies to all image builds.

docs.title: S3 cache
docs.text:
S3-compatible storage works with AWS S3, MinIO, Garage, and other S3-compatible services.

# hive.yml
cache:
  type: s3
  endpoint: http://garage:3900
  bucket: buildkit-cache
  region: garage
  access_key_id: <your-access-key>
  secret_access_key: <your-secret-key>
  use_path_style: true
Field Description type Must be s3 endpoint S3-compatible endpoint URL bucket Bucket name region S3 region access_key_id Access key secret_access_key Secret key use_path_style Use path-style addressing (required for MinIO, Garage, and most self-hosted S3)

docs.title: When to use S3
docs.text:
• You run builds across multiple machines or CI runners and need shared caching
  • You already have S3-compatible storage available (AWS, MinIO, Garage)
  • You want cache persistence independent of your container registry

docs.title: Setting up MinIO for local development
docs.text:
Using the pgsty/minio image for a lightweight local setup:

docker run -d \
  --name minio \
  -p 9000:9000 \
  -e MINIO_ROOT_USER=minioadmin \
  -e MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD=minioadmin \
  pgsty/minio server /data

cache:
  type: s3
  endpoint: http://localhost:9000
  bucket: buildkit-cache
  region: us-east-1
  access_key_id: <created-via-minio-admin-ui>
  secret_access_key: <created-via-minio-admin-ui>
  use_path_style: true

docs.title: Registry cache
docs.text:
Uses a container registry to store cache layers alongside your images.

# hive.yml
cache:
  type: registry
  ref: registry:5000/cache
  insecure: true
Field Description type Must be registry ref Registry reference for cache storage (e.g. registry:5000/cache) insecure Allow HTTP connections to the registry

docs.title: When to use registry cache
docs.text:
• You want a simpler setup without additional infrastructure
  • Your container registry supports OCI image manifests
  • You want cache stored in the same place as your images

Cache retention

Registry cache layers grow over time. Set up a retention policy on the cache repository (e.g. 3 weeks) to keep recent layers while discarding stale ones. See Clean up registry images with retention policies for per-provider setup instructions.

docs.title: How caching works
docs.text:
BuildKit uses the cache configuration for both importing (reading) and exporting (writing) cache layers:

  1. Before building, BuildKit checks the cache backend for existing layers that match the build context.
  2. Matching layers are reused, skipping the corresponding build steps.
  3. After building, all new layers are pushed to the cache backend.

Caching operates in max mode, meaning all intermediate layers are cached — not just the final image layers. This maximizes cache hits for multi-stage builds.

Cache errors are non-fatal. If the cache backend is unavailable, builds proceed without caching.

docs.title: No caching
docs.text: If no cache section is defined in hive.yml, builds run without caching. This is fine for local development but not recommended for CI.

docs.title: Build images with Chisel
docs.text:
[!WARNING] The Chisel build backend is highly experimental, like the Nix build backend. It is tested with small sample images only. Real projects may hit behaviors the samples do not cover. Try it, and file feedback at the issue tracker — any feedback is welcome.

Images in a ContainerHive project can define their filesystem with Chisel instead of a Dockerfile. Chisel cuts minimal package slices from the Ubuntu archives (see canonical/chisel-releases) and assembles them into a rootfs. ContainerHive resolves the project, cuts the rootfs through BuildKit, and pushes, tests, and documents the result like any other image.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
ContainerHive runs chisel cut inside a builder image through a custom BuildKit frontend:

  1. Discovery finds a chisel.yaml cut spec in the image directory and marks the image with the chisel build backend.
  2. generate renders the image directory, copying the cut spec, the custom slices/ directory, the rootfs/ directory, and the test config into dist/.
  3. build prepares a cached toolchain stage on top of the builder image: git, ca-certificates, and the chisel binary, each only when the image lacks it. A second stage then runs chisel cut --release <local-checkout> in /src; the cut rootfs becomes the image filesystem on an empty base.
  4. Everything else is unchanged: OCI labels, the S3 or registry build cache, multi-arch pushes, SBOMs, and structure tests run like on Dockerfile builds.

Only the BuildKit worker pulls the builder image and the chisel tool binary. Neither ch nor the CI pipeline needs Chisel or git installed. ContainerHive does not bundle a builder image; the default one comes from the helper-images project.

docs.title: The cut spec contract
docs.text:
The build entrypoint is chisel.yaml next to image.yml:

release: ubuntu-24.04
slices:
  - base-files_base
  - base-files_release-info
  - ca-certificates_data
  - hello_bins
  • release names a branch of the canonical chisel-releases repository, for example ubuntu-24.04. Chisel cuts release ubuntu-24.04 for the ubuntu-24.04 branch in the archive.
  • slices lists the slices to cut in chisel notation <package>_<slice>. Chisel resolves slice dependencies (the essential edges) automatically.

A JSON schema for the cut spec is published to SchemaNest and can be referenced directly at schema-nest.timo-reymann.de/api/schema/json-schema/containerhive-chisel/latest.

An optional ignore field lets chisel cut unstable or unmaintained releases, same behavior as chisel cut --ignore. See the cut command reference.

[!NOTE] A common naming collision: Chisel itself also has a chisel.yaml — the release manifest inside a chisel-releases checkout. The two formats are unrelated. ContainerHive's chisel.yaml is a cut spec that drives the build; the release manifest lives inside the release checkout that chisel cut consumes.

docs.title: Release sources
docs.text:
The release supports two forms:

  • A branch name — release: ubuntu-24.04 clones the named branch of canonical/chisel-releases. The build tracks the branch head, like Chisel's own release fetch.
  • A git mapping — for pinned and custom releases:
release:
  git: https://github.com/canonical/chisel-releases
  ref: "0a817bd"  # commit, tag, or branch

A missing ref checks out the default branch. Discovery logs a warning, because the build is then not reproducible. Pin a commit for release workflows.

[!TIP] Rebuilds fetch the release checkout incrementally from a cached clone, so an unchanged release skips the checkout and the deb downloads. The git path also works offline once the clone and the deb cache are warm, and it avoids the HTTP check that Chisel's built-in release fetch makes on every run.

docs.title: Custom slice definitions
docs.text:
An optional slices/ folder next to the cut spec holds custom slice definitions in the chisel-releases format — one YAML per package, with package:, slices:, and the contents paths. The build overlays the folder on the resolved release before the cut, so the new packages resolve like release definitions:

images/hello/
├── chisel.yaml
└── slices/
    └── mypkg.yaml

Cut a locally defined package like any other: add mypkg_bins to slices in the cut spec.

docs.title: Configure the backend in image.yml
docs.text:
Most images need no extra configuration:

description: "My tool image, cut from Ubuntu slices"
build: chisel

tags:
  - name: 1.0.0

Set build: chisel explicitly, or let discovery pick the backend: a chisel.yaml that is the only build entrypoint uses the Chisel backend automatically. A cut spec next to a flake.nix or a Dockerfile is ambiguous and fails discovery; set build in that case.

The chisel block configures the backend:

build: chisel

chisel:
  builder_image: "ghcr.io/containerhive/helper-images/chisel:1.5"  # base image for the build stages (default)
  chisel_version: "v1.5.1"       # chisel tool version, only downloaded when the builder image ships another one
  extra_args: []                 # extra chisel cut arguments

The default builder image is the chisel image of ContainerHive/helper-images. It ships chisel, git and ca-certificates, so the toolchain stage installs and downloads nothing. That repository is itself a ContainerHive project and publishes one tag per chisel release series (1.5, 1.4, ...).

The toolchain stage adds only what the builder image lacks:

  • git and ca-certificates are installed with apt-get when missing, so such an image has to be Debian or Ubuntu based. An image that already contains both needs no package manager.
  • chisel is downloaded from the GitHub release when the image ships no chisel, or ships another version than chisel_version. An image declares the chisel it ships with the chisel.version label. Without chisel_version, a shipped chisel is used as is; without a label, the default version is downloaded.

A plain ubuntu:24.04 still works as builder image.

Because a cut spec carries no Dockerfile instructions, the runtime configuration of the image looks like this:

config:
  entrypoint: [ "/bin/hello" ]
  cmd: [ "--help" ] 
  env:
    TOOL_HOME: /var/lib/my-tool
  user: "1000:1000"
  working_dir: /workspace

Set working_dir, user, cmd, env, and entrypoint as needed. Unset fields stay empty.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text: Variants keep working: place a chisel.yaml into the variant directory and configure the variant like an image, with variant-level build, chisel, and config blocks.

docs.title: Parent images
docs.text:
A cut build can start from a parent image rootfs instead of an empty base. Set chisel.parent on the image or variant:

build: chisel
depends_on:
  - base

chisel:
  parent: "__hive__/base:1.0"

The value takes three forms:

  • __hive__/<name>:<tag> — another image of the project. ContainerHive resolves it from the local build cache like a Dockerfile dependency; CI resolves it from the registry. The build order derives from the reference; an explicit depends_on is not required.
  • __hive_parent__ — the variant placeholder. Only valid inside a variant: it resolves to the base tag __hive__/<name>:<tag> of the same image.
  • Any other value is a plain image reference, for example ubuntu:22.04. It resolves through the registry and is digest-pinned like the builder image.

The build mounts the parent rootfs at /parent and copies it into the image first, so the cut output overlays the parent. The slice files land on top of the parent files. An image-config-level merge applies as well: entrypoint, cmd, env, user and working dir inherit from the parent unless the config block sets them. Symlinks stay symlinks: the cut output is copied verbatim, and only the parent merge resolves links into the target directory.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Chisel caches two things inside one BuildKit worker container: the git checkout of the release repo, and the downloaded .deb packages. Set cache: false to opt out when a daemon has no place for a growing cache:

build: chisel

chisel:
  cache: false

The default is on. The cache lives inside one BuildKit daemon. A fresh daemon starts cold, and the registry or S3 build cache does not carry it — the images themselves are what the build cache stores. The cache grows with the deb churn of the archive; prune the hive-chisel-cache mount when it grows too large.

docs.title: Static rootfs files
docs.text:
A rootfs/ directory next to the cut spec contributes static image content — files chisel cannot know, like configuration files. The build assembles the filesystem in this order:

  1. The parent rootfs (when chisel.parent is set).
  2. The cut slice files.
  3. The rootfs/ files.

rootfs/ files overwrite slice files on the same path. structure test configs and OCI labels behave the same on all backends.

docs.title: Templating
docs.text:
A cut spec renders through the ContainerHive template engine like any other build entrypoint. Name the templated spec chisel.yaml.gotpl; generate renders it and writes the result as chisel.yaml. A plain chisel.yaml is copied as is without template processing.

chisel.yaml.gotpl
release: ubuntu-{{ .Versions.ubuntu }}
slices:
  - base-files_base
  - hello_bins

Rendering happens at generate time. A new build arg value re-renders the spec and invalidates the build cache, by design.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Ubuntu Pro archives (esm-apps, esm-infra, fips) are not supported until someone requests them. FIPS builds need credentials this backend does not wire up yet.
  • Release format support follows the chisel tool version: the pinned chisel_version opens the formats, see the compatibility matrix.
  • Multi-platform builds run under emulation on non-native machines, like the Nix backend. Chisel publishes no linux/386 tool binary, so linux/386 images fail the build with a clear error.
  • The cut cannot read the parent rootfs while it runs. The parent merge happens in the build script afterwards.
  • The release checkout and the deb cache live in one cache mount. Chisel cuts on one daemon are serialized, so concurrent builds never race on the release checkout.

docs.title: Generate CI pipelines
docs.text: ContainerHive generates CI pipeline configurations from your project definition, so you don't have to maintain pipeline YAML by hand.

docs.title: Generating CI pipelines
docs.text:
Use template ci to generate a pipeline for your CI provider:

ch template ci --provider gitlab --output .gitlab-ci.yml
ch template ci --provider github --output .github/workflows/build.yml

docs.title: Supported providers
docs.text: Provider Flag value Output GitLab CI gitlab GitLab CI pipeline YAML GitHub Actions github GitHub Actions workflow YAML

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. ContainerHive discovers your project and resolves image dependencies.
  2. Images are grouped into stages based on their dependency depth — images at the same depth can build in parallel.
  3. For each image, the pipeline includes jobs for building (per-platform), creating multi-arch manifests, and running tests.
  4. If an image has a latest_alias configured, the highest semantic version tag is automatically retagged as the specified alias (e.g., latest, stable).
  5. The generated pipeline references the ContainerHive container image to run all commands.
  6. Before builds, Dockerfiles are linted with hadolint (enabled by default). Lint failures gate the build stage.
  7. After successful builds, an HTML and JSON report is generated and published to GitHub Pages or GitLab Pages.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Flag Description --provider CI provider (gitlab or github) — required --output Output file path (default: stdout) --template-dir Custom template directory to override built-in templates --artifacts Upload/download build artifacts between jobs --version ContainerHive CLI version to use (default: current version) --image-name Container image name for the CLI (default: ghcr.io/containerhive/containerhive for github, registry.gitlab.com/containerhive/containerhive for gitlab)

docs.title: Example with custom image
docs.text:
ch template ci \
  --provider github \
  --output .github/workflows/build.yml \
  --image-name ghcr.io/containerhive/containerhive \
  --version v1.0.0 \
  --artifacts

docs.title: Custom templates
docs.text:
For use cases beyond CI pipelines, the template custom command renders any Go template with full access to the project context.

ch template custom --template my-template.gotpl --output output.yml

The --output value is itself rendered as a Go template with the same context as the template file, so the destination can be derived from the project:

ch template custom --template image.gotpl --output 'foo/{{ .Image.Name }}.yml'

When the output path references .Image, the template is rendered once per image and one file is written per image — .Image is bound to the current image in both the output path and the template content. Without .Image, a single render writes a single file (and .Image is not available in the content). Missing parent directories in the output path are created automatically.

docs.title: Template context
docs.text:
Custom templates receive a CIContext with the following fields:

Field Type Description Images list All images (see below) Platforms list All unique platforms across all images Stages list Ordered build stages (build-<image>, test-<image>, manifest-<image>) Config object Registry and cache configuration (see below) Artifacts bool Whether build artifacts are passed between jobs (set by template ci --artifacts) TemplateOptions map Merged template options (defaults + hive.yml), same values the option(key) function returns HasTagRanges bool Whether any image defines tag_ranges TagRangeUnits int Total version-cache tag units across all images (0 unless HasTagRanges is true) Command string The ch template ci command line — only set by template ci, empty in custom templates Version string CH CLI version used in CI templates — only set by template ci ImageName string Container image name for the CH CLI — only set by template ci ProjectPath string --project value when it is not . — only set by template ci

Each image in Images provides:

Field Type Description Name string Image name Tags list All tags including variant-suffixed tags (base + variants) Aliases map Alias name to the exact tag it points at: semantic version series aliases (1.2.3 → 1.2, 1) and latest_alias, including variant-suffixed ones. Same resolution as the registry retagging step Dependencies list Names of images this image depends on Depth int Dependency depth (0 = no dependencies) Platforms list Target platforms: union of the base tag and variant platforms. Plain linux platforms are shortened to the architecture (amd64), others keep their full value (linux/arm/v7); use platform_id for identifiers ReadmePath string Path to the image's README.md, empty if it has none. Load the content with read_file ShardUnits int Number of shard units (base + variant tags) — the useful max BuildShards int Effective parallel for build jobs (min(ci_build_shards, ShardUnits)) TestShards int Effective parallel for test jobs (min(ci_test_shards, ShardUnits))

Config exposes the project registry and cache configuration:

Field Type Description Config.Registry.Address string Container registry address Config.Registry.DockerMediaTypes bool Force Docker-scheme media types (null = auto-detect) Config.RegistryHost() string Registry hostname without path (e.g. docker.io/timoreymann → docker.io) Config.Cache.Type string Cache backend: s3 or registry Config.Cache.Endpoint string S3 endpoint URL Config.Cache.Bucket string S3 bucket name Config.Cache.Region string S3 region Config.Cache.AccessKeyId string S3 access key ID Config.Cache.SecretAccessKey string S3 secret access key — available, but avoid rendering it into committed files Config.Cache.UsePathStyle bool Use path-style S3 URLs Config.Cache.Ref string Registry cache ref (e.g. registry:5000/cache) Config.Cache.Insecure bool Allow insecure registry connections

Note

Config.Registry and Config.Cache are pointers and render as <no value> when unset — guard with {{ with .Config.Cache }}...{{ end }}. Registry.DockerMediaTypes is a tri-state: unset means auto-detect.

The context also provides helper methods, callable like functions:

Method Description ChCmd() The ch command prefix, including -p <project> when a project path is set Dist() The dist directory path, prefixed with the project path when set VersionCacheDir() The tag_ranges version cache path, prefixed with the project path when set

docs.title: Template functions
docs.text:
Templates have access to Sprig functions plus:

Function Description resolve_base(name, tag) Produces an internal image reference (__hive__/name:tag) for inter-image dependencies option(key) Returns the value of a template option from hive.yml, or empty string if not set platform_id(platform) Turns a platform into a value safe for job IDs and artifact names: amd64 stays amd64, linux/arm/v7 becomes linux-arm-v7 platform_dir(platform) Returns the dist/ directory name of a platform, e.g. linux-amd64 for amd64 platform_arch(platform) Returns the architecture of a platform, e.g. arm64 for linux/arm64/v8 read_file(path) Returns the content of a file, or an empty string for an empty path — e.g. {{ .Image.ReadmePath \| read_file }}. Fails if the file does not exist

docs.title: Example custom template
docs.text:
{{- range .Images }}
Image: {{ .Name }}
  Tags: {{ range .Tags }}{{ . }}, {{ end }}
  Platforms: {{ range .Platforms }}{{ . }}, {{ end }}
  Dependencies: {{ range .Dependencies }}{{ . }}, {{ end }}
{{ end }}

docs.title: Overriding built-in CI templates
docs.text:
You can override the built-in CI templates by providing a custom template directory:

ch template ci --provider gitlab --template-dir ./my-templates --output .gitlab-ci.yml

The directory should contain .gotpl files following the same structure as the built-in templates. Files in the custom directory take precedence over the built-in ones.

docs.title: Built-in template structure
docs.text:
templates/<provider>/
├── pipeline.yml.gotpl   (or workflow.yml.gotpl for GitHub)
├── build-job.yml.gotpl
├── lint-job.yml.gotpl
├── manifest-job.yml.gotpl
└── test-job.yml.gotpl

The entrypoint template includes the job templates as partials using {{ template "build-job.yml.gotpl" . }}.

docs.title: The generate command
docs.text:
Before building or generating CI configs, run generate to discover the project and render all configurations to dist/:

ch generate

This processes hive.yml and all image.yml definitions, renders Dockerfiles and test templates, and prepares the dist/ directory for subsequent build, test, and sbom commands.

docs.title: Report generation
docs.text:
By default, the generated CI pipeline includes a report job that runs after all build jobs complete. This job generates:

  • dist/report.html — Interactive HTML report with image details, tags, platforms, and SBOM data
  • dist/report.json — Machine-readable JSON report

docs.title: GitHub Pages
docs.text: The HTML report is automatically deployed to GitHub Pages. Your repository must have Pages enabled in settings with the source set to "GitHub Actions".

docs.title: GitLab Pages
docs.text: The report is uploaded as a GitLab Pages artifact and exposed as "ContainerHive Report" in the merge request widget. The JSON report is also available as an artifact.

docs.title: Lint job
docs.text: By default, the generated CI pipeline includes a lint job that runs after the generate stage and before any build stages. This job lints all plain Dockerfiles in the project using hadolint via ch lint.

docs.title: GitLab Code Quality report
docs.text:
For GitLab CI, the lint job produces a Code Quality report artifact that GitLab renders inline on merge requests. The report uses the codeclimate output format:

ch lint --format codeclimate=gl-code-quality-report.json

docs.title: GitHub Actions annotations
docs.text:
For GitHub Actions, use the github-actions output format to emit annotations inline on pull request diffs:

ch lint --format github-actions

Lint failures still cause the job to fail and gate subsequent build jobs. Without the --format flag, findings only appear in the workflow log — using --format github-actions makes them visible on the changed lines in the PR.

docs.title: Disabling linting
docs.text:
To disable the lint job entirely, set ci_lint to false in your hive.yml:

template_options:
  ci_lint: false

docs.title: Reducing SBOM size
docs.text:
syft attaches CPEs to every component by default, which is a meaningful contributor to SBOM size on images with many packages. Set ci_sbom_generate_cpes to false to pass --no-cpe to ch sbom in the generated GitLab CI pipeline, trading CPE-based vulnerability matching for a smaller artifact — useful if you're running into GitLab's SBOM artifact size limits:

template_options:
  ci_sbom_generate_cpes: "false"

docs.title: Cancelling outdated pipelines
docs.text: By default, when a new pipeline is triggered on the same branch, in-progress pipelines from earlier commits are automatically cancelled to save CI resources. This behaviour is controlled by the ci_cancel_outdated option.

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
The generated workflow uses a concurrency group scoped to the workflow and branch. On a push to the default branch, a new run cancels the previous in-progress run. Pull request runs use a unique group per run, so PR behaviour is unchanged (no cancellation, no queueing).

Requires actions: read permission (included in the generated workflow).

docs.title: GitLab CI
docs.text:
The generated pipeline sets workflow:auto_cancel:on_new_commit: interruptible (GitLab 16.9+) and marks all jobs as interruptible: true via the default block (GitLab 15.9+). This forces auto-cancel of superseded in-progress pipelines on the same ref, regardless of the project-level "Auto-cancel redundant pipelines" setting.

Note: GitLab's auto-cancel mechanism applies per ref. A new push to a merge request also cancels that MR's superseded pipeline. There is no clean way to restrict cancellation to the default branch only.

To disable, set ci_cancel_outdated to false in your hive.yml:

template_options:
  ci_cancel_outdated: "false"

docs.title: Docker-in-Docker for test jobs
docs.text:
ch test needs a Docker daemon. The generated test jobs start it as a dind service using the rootless dind-rootless helper image, so the service runs without a privileged security context. This is what makes the pipeline work on Kubernetes runners that forbid privileged pods.

On the Kubernetes executor the rootless daemon needs a user mapping that fits the pod (hostUsers: false), which is a cluster-side setting. Use the privileged docker:dind image, or your own mirror, with ci_dind_image:

template_options:
  ci_dind_image: docker:dind

docker:dind needs the runner to allow a privileged Docker-in-Docker service. Setting the option does not replace hostUsers: false on a runner that forbids privileged pods; there the daemon does not start.

The generated GitHub Actions workflow starts the same image as a container on the runner VM, with --privileged.

docs.title: Sharding build and test jobs
docs.text:
For GitLab CI, ci_build_shards and ci_test_shards set an upper bound on parallel: N for each build/test job. The actual value is capped per image to the number of shard units (base + variant tags) that image has, so images with fewer tags than the configured value never spawn empty jobs that no-op. See Split work across shards for the full picture; the template option is set the same way as ci_lint above:

Generated build and test jobs are split by platform and pass --platform to ch, which skips tags and variants that do not support that platform (see Selecting platforms). Generated test jobs run on matching architecture runners. In GitLab, each job extends a shared .test-<platform> (and .build-<platform>) base, which can be extended in your root .gitlab-ci.yml to add runner tags. <platform> is the platform with linux/ dropped for plain architectures and / replaced by - otherwise: amd64, arm64, linux-arm-v7, windows-amd64. Job IDs and artifact names use the same form.

.test-arm64:
  tags: [my-arm64-runner]

template_options:
  ci_build_shards: "5"
  ci_test_shards: "5"

docs.title: Registry retention
docs.text:
Every generated pipeline pushes per-platform intermediate images and, when using --build-id, snapshot manifests and aliases into the registry. These accumulate over time — even for MRs that are never merged. Since ch test and ch finalize need to pull these images, skipping pushes is not an option. Instead, configure a registry-level retention policy to automatically clean up snapshot images after a few days.

See Clean up registry images with retention policies for per-provider setup instructions.

docs.title: Use the CLI
docs.text:
ContainerHive's behavior can be controlled with various commands and flags.

You can get a full list by running

ch --help

docs.title: Global Flags
docs.text:
Flag Description --project, -p Project root directory --build-id Build ID appended to tags as -build.<id> --log-level Log level (debug, info, warn, error) — sourced from LOG_LEVEL env (default: info) --generate, -g Run ch generate before the command --refresh-versions Ignore the tag_ranges version cache TTL and refetch every external version source — sourced from CH_REFRESH_VERSIONS env

See Environment variables for everything ch reads from the environment.

docs.title: generate
docs.text:
Discover project and render configurations to dist/.

ch generate

This must run before build. It parses hive.yml and all image definitions.

docs.title: build
docs.text:
Build container images with BuildKit.

ch build [image:tag patterns...]
Flag Description --registry Use registry from config (auto-enabled in CI) --platform Target platform(s) to build (e.g. linux/amd64). Selects within the platforms configured in hive.yml/image.yml; tags and variants that support none of them are skipped. A platform that nothing configures is an error --max-shards Total number of shards to split work across — sourced from CI_NODE_TOTAL env (default: 1) --current-shard This shard's 1-based index — sourced from CI_NODE_INDEX env (default: 1)

You can filter which images to build by passing image:tag patterns as arguments. In CI environments, the registry is auto-enabled. See Sharding for --max-shards/--current-shard.

docs.title: test
docs.text:
Run container structure tests on built images.

ch test [image:tag patterns...]
Flag Description --build Run build before tests --platform Target platform(s) to test (e.g. linux/amd64). Selects within the configured platforms like build --platform; also applies to --build --max-shards Total number of shards to split work across — sourced from CI_NODE_TOTAL env (default: 1) --current-shard This shard's 1-based index — sourced from CI_NODE_INDEX env (default: 1)

See Sharding for --max-shards/--current-shard.

You can combine --build with --generate to run the full pipeline in one command:

ch test --generate --build

Uses container-structure-test to validate built images against test definitions.

docs.title: sbom
docs.text:
Generate Software Bill of Materials for built images.

ch sbom [image:tag patterns...]
Flag Description --platform Target platform(s) to generate SBOMs for (e.g. linux/amd64). Selects within the configured platforms like build --platform --workers Number of concurrent workers for SBOM generation (default: 4) --no-cpe Skip CPE generation to reduce SBOM size (may reduce vulnerability match accuracy for CPE-based scanners) --max-shards Total number of shards to split work across — sourced from CI_NODE_TOTAL env (default: 1) --current-shard This shard's 1-based index — sourced from CI_NODE_INDEX env (default: 1)

Generates CycloneDX JSON format SBOMs using Syft as a Go library. No external tooling required. See Sharding for --max-shards/--current-shard — useful when many tags and variants push a single job's SBOM artifacts past a CI provider's size limit.

docs.title: finalize
docs.text:
Create multi-arch manifests and semantic version alias tags in the registry.

ch finalize [image:tag patterns...]

Creates manifests from platform-specific images and applies semantic version alias tagging. Requires a running registry.

docs.title: verify
docs.text:
Verify project structure.

ch verify

Validates hive.yml and image definitions. Useful as a quick check before building.

docs.title: lint
docs.text:
Lint Dockerfiles in the project with hadolint. The hadolint binary is embedded in ch — no separate install required.

ch lint
Flag Description --failure-threshold Lowest severity that causes a non-zero exit (error, warning, info, style, ignore). Overrides lint.failure_threshold from hive.yml. Defaults to error. --format Output format(s). Repeatable flag. Supported values: terminal, github-actions, codeclimate=<path>. Default: terminal.

Findings are printed to stdout in path:line:column level code: message format by default. Templated Dockerfiles (files with a templating extension such as Dockerfile.gotpl) are skipped — hadolint cannot parse Go template syntax — and a warning is logged for each skipped file. Per-variant Dockerfiles are linted alongside the parent image.

Configure hadolint behaviour with a lint: block in hive.yml. See Hive configuration.

docs.title: Output formats
docs.text:
One or more --format flags can be specified:

ch lint --format terminal
ch lint --format github-actions
ch lint --format codeclimate=gl-code-quality-report.json
ch lint --format terminal --format github-actions --format codeclimate=gl-code-quality-report.json

docs.title: terminal
docs.text: Colored text output to stdout. Used by default when no --format is given.

docs.title: github-actions
docs.text:
Emits GitHub Actions workflow command annotations to stdout, making findings appear inline on the diff in pull requests. Severities are mapped from hadolint to workflow commands as follows:

hadolint GitHub Actions command error ::error warning ::warning info ::notice style ::notice

The annotation includes the repo-relative file path, line and column numbers, the rule code as the title, and the finding message as the body. Messages are sanitized to prevent injection of false workflow commands.

Wire it into a GitHub Actions workflow step:

- name: Lint Dockerfiles
  run: ch lint --format github-actions

docs.title: codeclimate=<path>
docs.text:
Writes a Code Climate–compatible JSON report that GitLab CI can render inline on merge requests. Requires a file path suffix (e.g., codeclimate=gl-code-quality-report.json). Severities are mapped from hadolint to Code Climate as follows:

hadolint Code Climate error blocker warning major info minor style info

Wire it into .gitlab-ci.yml like any other code-quality artifact:

lint:
  script:
    - ch lint --format codeclimate=gl-code-quality-report.json
  artifacts:
    when: always
    reports:
      codequality: gl-code-quality-report.json

Every parsed finding lands in the report — even ones below the failure threshold — so GitLab surfaces the full picture while the command's exit code still reflects the threshold.

docs.title: template ci
docs.text:
Generate CI pipeline configuration.

ch template ci --provider <provider> --output <path>
Flag Description --provider CI provider (gitlab or github) --output Output file (default: stdout) --template-dir Custom template directory (overrides built-in templates) --artifacts Upload/download build artifacts between jobs --version CH CLI version to use in CI templates (default: current CLI version) --image-name Container image name for the CH CLI (default: ghcr.io/containerhive/containerhive for --provider github, registry.gitlab.com/containerhive/containerhive for --provider gitlab)

docs.title: template custom
docs.text:
Render custom Go templates with project context.

ch template custom --template <path.gotpl> --output <path>
Flag Description --template Path to Go template file (.gotpl) --output Output path rendered as a Go template (default: stdout). References to .Image render once per image, one file each

docs.title: wait
docs.text:
Wait for infrastructure dependencies to become available.

ch wait
Flag Description --buildkitd Wait for BuildKit daemon (uses $BUILDKIT_HOST, default tcp://127.0.0.1:8372) --docker-socket Wait for Docker daemon (uses $DOCKER_HOST, default unix:///var/run/docker.sock) --timeout Maximum time to wait (default: 1m)

docs.title: login
docs.text:
Log in to a container registry.

ch login <registry> -u <username> -p <password>
Flag Description --username, -u Username --password, -p Password --password-stdin Take the password from stdin

docs.title: dev buildkitd
docs.text:
Manage a local BuildKit daemon container for development. See Local development for full details.

ch dev buildkitd start
ch dev buildkitd stop
ch dev buildkitd status
ch dev buildkitd logs

start flags:

Flag Description --image BuildKit image to use (image:tag). Defaults to the version configured in hive.yml template_options or the bundled version --port Host port to bind --timeout Maximum time to wait for buildkitd to become ready (default: 1m)

stop flags:

Flag Description --remove Also remove the container after stopping

logs flags:

Flag Description --follow, -f Follow log output

docs.title: report
docs.text:
Generate an HTML or JSON report of container images.

ch report
Flag Description --output Output file path (default: dist/report.html) --json Output JSON instead of HTML

Generates a report containing information about all configured images, including their build status, dependencies, and metadata.

docs.title: Customizing the report
docs.text: To customize the look of the HTML report, set report.styleSheet in your hive.yml to a path pointing at a CSS file. The contents of that file are embedded verbatim into the generated HTML via a <style> block. See Report theme for the full list of overridable variables.

docs.title: URL parameters
docs.text:
The HTML report supports the following query parameters:

Parameter Description ?hide-header Hides the top header bar. Useful when embedding the report in an iframe or dashboard.

docs.title: license
docs.text:
Show third-party license notices.

ch license

docs.title: mcp
docs.text:
Start a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for AI tool integration.

ch mcp

See MCP integration for full details.

docs.title: Write your Dockerfiles
docs.text: ContainerHive renders Dockerfiles as part of ch generate. This page covers how versions, build arguments, secrets, and inter-image dependencies work in your Dockerfiles.

docs.title: Plain Dockerfiles vs templates
docs.text:
ContainerHive supports both plain Dockerfiles and Go template Dockerfiles:

  • Dockerfile — copied as-is. Versions and build args are passed as Docker ARGs.
  • Dockerfile.gotpl — rendered as a Go template before building. Has access to template variables and functions in addition to Docker ARGs.

The .gotpl extension is optional. Use it only when you need Go template features like resolve_base or conditional logic. For most cases, plain Dockerfiles with ARG are sufficient.

Info

The same applies to test files: test.yml is copied as-is, test.yml.gotpl is rendered as a template.

docs.title: Using versions
docs.text:
Versions defined in image.yml are automatically converted to Docker build arguments with an uppercase _VERSION suffix. Hyphens in the key name are replaced with underscores.

Given this image.yml:

versions:
  dotnet-sdk-channel: "8.0"
  nodejs: "24"

The following build arguments are available in your Dockerfile:

ARG DOTNET_SDK_CHANNEL_VERSION
ARG NODEJS_VERSION

RUN install-dotnet --channel "${DOTNET_SDK_CHANNEL_VERSION}"
RUN setup-node "${NODEJS_VERSION}"

Tag-level versions override image-level versions:

versions:
  app: latest

tags:
  - name: 1.0.0
    versions:
      app: 1.0.0   # overrides "latest" for this tag

docs.title: Using build arguments
docs.text:
Build arguments from image.yml are passed directly to Docker without any name transformation:

build_args:
  foo: bar

ARG foo
RUN echo "${foo}"

docs.title: Using secrets
docs.text:
Secrets defined in image.yml are mounted via BuildKit's secret mount mechanism:

secrets:
  my_credentials:
    source: env       # read from environment variable
    value: API_KEY    # name of the env var

Access them in your Dockerfile with --mount=type=secret:

RUN --mount=type=secret,id=my_credentials \
    cat /run/secrets/my_credentials

docs.title: Secret sources
docs.text: Source Description env Resolves value as an environment variable name (supports $VAR and ${VAR} syntax) plain Uses value as the literal secret content vault Resolves value as a Vault path (vault://<path>#<field>)

docs.title: Inter-image dependencies
docs.text:
When your image depends on another image in the same project, use the __hive__/ prefix in FROM:

FROM __hive__/ubuntu:22.04
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl

ContainerHive resolves these references to local OCI layout contexts during the build, so inter-image dependencies don't need to be pushed to an external registry.

docs.title: Variant parent references
docs.text:
Variants that build on top of their base image can use __hive_parent__:

FROM __hive_parent__
ARG NODEJS_VERSION
RUN setup-node "${NODEJS_VERSION}"

This is automatically replaced with the correct __hive__/<image>:<tag> reference for the current tag during ch generate.

docs.title: Go template Dockerfiles
docs.text:
When using the .gotpl extension, you get access to the full template context:

Variable Description {{ .Versions.key }} Version values from image/tag/variant {{ .BuildArgs.key }} Build arguments from image/tag/variant {{ .ImageName }} The image name

docs.title: Template functions
docs.text:
All Sprig functions are available, plus:

Function Description resolve_base "name" "tag" Produces __hive__/name:tag — use this instead of hardcoding __hive__/ references

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
FROM {{ resolve_base "ubuntu" .Versions.ubuntu_tag }}
RUN echo "Building {{ .ImageName }}"

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
image.yml:

tags:
  - name: 8.0.100
    versions:
      dotnet-sdk-channel: 8.0.1xx
  - name: 8.0.200
    versions:
      dotnet-sdk-channel: 8.0.2xx

variants:
  - name: node
    tag_suffix: -node
    versions:
      nodejs: "24"

secrets:
  foo:
    value: bar

depends_on:
  - ubuntu

platforms:
  - linux/amd64

Dockerfile:

FROM __hive__/ubuntu:22.04
ARG DOTNET_SDK_CHANNEL_VERSION
RUN curl -L https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh -o /usr/bin/install-dotnet \
    && chmod +x /usr/bin/install-dotnet \
    && install-dotnet --channel "${DOTNET_SDK_CHANNEL_VERSION}" --install-dir /usr/share/dotnet

RUN --mount=type=secret,id=foo \
    cat /run/secrets/foo

node/Dockerfile (variant):

FROM __hive_parent__
ARG NODEJS_VERSION
RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install --no-install-recommends -y nodejs=${NODEJS_VERSION}

docs.title: Filter images and tags
docs.text: Most ContainerHive commands accept image:tag filters as positional arguments to target specific images or tags instead of processing the entire project.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
ch <command> [image[:tag] ...]
Pattern Matches (none) All images and tags ubuntu All tags of the ubuntu image ubuntu:24.04 Only tag 24.04 of image ubuntu ubuntu:24.04 alpine:3.20 Both specified image:tag combinations

docs.title: Commands that support filtering
docs.text:
• ch build — build only matching images
  • ch test — test only matching images
  • ch sbom — generate SBOMs for matching images
  • ch finalize — create manifests for matching images

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Build a single image:

ch build ubuntu

Build a specific tag:

ch build ubuntu:24.04

Test multiple images:

ch test ubuntu:24.04 python:3.13.7

Generate SBOMs for one image:

ch sbom dotnet

docs.title: Variant tags
docs.text:
Variant tags include the tag suffix defined in image.yml. To filter for a variant, specify the full tag including the suffix:

ch build dotnet:8.0.200-node

docs.title: Matching rules
docs.text:
• If no filters are provided, all images and tags are processed.
  • Image name matching is exact — no wildcards or glob patterns.
  • Tag matching is exact — no wildcards or glob patterns.
  • Specifying only an image name matches all tags of that image.
  • Multiple filters are combined with OR logic — an image:tag matches if it matches any filter.

docs.title: Sharding
docs.text: Filters and sharding compose: filters select which images and tags are in scope at all, and sharding partitions whatever remains across parallel CI jobs.

docs.title: Local development
docs.text: The ch dev command group provides convenience helpers for running a local development environment. This removes the need to set up infrastructure manually when iterating on images.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
A Docker-compatible daemon must be reachable. By default the Docker socket at /var/run/docker.sock is used. Set $DOCKER_HOST to point at a different daemon, including Podman:

export DOCKER_HOST=unix:///run/user/1000/podman/podman.sock

docs.title: BuildKit daemon
docs.text: ch dev buildkitd manages a local BuildKit daemon container named containerhive-buildkitd.

docs.title: Start
docs.text:
ch dev buildkitd start

This will:

  1. Pull the buildkitd image if not present locally.
  2. Create and start a privileged container listening on TCP.
  3. Wait until the daemon is ready to accept connections.
  4. Print the BUILDKIT_HOST export line.
export BUILDKIT_HOST=tcp://127.0.0.1:8372

Evaluate this in your shell to make subsequent ch build invocations use the local daemon:

eval $(ch dev buildkitd start)
ch build
Flag Default Description --image (see below) Full image:tag to use for the buildkitd container --port 8372 Host port to bind --timeout 1m How long to wait for the daemon to become ready

docs.title: Image version
docs.text:
By default the image is resolved from your project's template_options in hive.yml, using the same ci_buildkit_image and ci_buildkit_version keys that control the version used in generated CI pipelines. This keeps your local daemon in sync with CI.

If no overrides are configured, the version is taken from the github.com/moby/buildkit dependency in go.mod.

# hive.yml — pin the same version locally and in CI
template_options:
  ci_buildkit_version: v0.19.0

Use --image to override the full reference for a one-off run:

ch dev buildkitd start --image moby/buildkit:v0.19.0

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
ch dev buildkitd status

Shows the container state, image, bound port, and the BUILDKIT_HOST value to use.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
ch dev buildkitd logs
ch dev buildkitd logs --follow
Flag Description --follow, -f Stream log output until interrupted

docs.title: Stop
docs.text:
ch dev buildkitd stop
ch dev buildkitd stop --remove
Flag Description --remove Also remove the container after stopping

Without --remove the container is only stopped and can be started again with ch dev buildkitd start.

docs.title: Integration with AI Agents
docs.text: ContainerHive provides an MCP (Model Context Protocol) integration that enables AI assistants to manage container images programmatically.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Start the MCP server:

ch mcp --project /path/to/project

The server uses stdio transport, making it compatible with MCP clients like Claude Code, Cursor, and other AI assistants.

docs.title: AI Usage
docs.text:
ContainerHive's MCP server enables AI assistants to interact with your container project. When configured, AI can:

  • List and inspect images — Query all configured images, their variants, tags, and versions
  • Get dependencies — Understand build order by retrieving forward/reverse dependencies
  • Add new images — Create new image directories with starter Dockerfiles and configuration
  • Add variants — Extend existing images with new variants (e.g., -slim, -alpine)
  • Query schemas — Retrieve JSON schemas for validation and autocomplete
  • Search documentation — Find relevant docs within your project context
