docs.title: Build multi-platform images
docs.text: ContainerHive builds images for multiple architectures in a single workflow and creates multi-arch manifests so consumers pull the right image automatically.

docs.title: Configuring platforms
docs.text: Platforms are configured at three levels, with the most specific taking precedence:

docs.title: Project-level (default for all images)
docs.text:
# hive.yml
platforms:
  - linux/amd64
  - linux/arm64

docs.title: Image-level (override for a specific image)
docs.text:
# image.yml
platforms:
  - linux/amd64

docs.title: Variant-level (override for a specific variant)
docs.text:
# image.yml
variants:
  - name: slim
    tag_suffix: -slim
    platforms:
      - linux/amd64

The resolution order is: variant > image > project. If a variant defines platforms, those are used. Otherwise the image-level platforms are used, falling back to the project-level default.

docs.title: Selecting platforms with --platform
docs.text:
ch build, ch test and ch sbom accept --platform to work on a subset of platforms, for example one platform per CI job. The flag selects within the resolved list, it does not replace it. A tag or variant whose resolved platforms do not include the requested platform is skipped.

With the slim variant above restricted to linux/amd64, ch build --platform linux/arm64 builds the arm64 base tags but skips -slim. Each skipped tag is logged. If no tag selected by the filters (and shard) supports the platform, the command logs a warning, does nothing and exits successfully.

Requesting a platform that no project, image or variant configures (for example a typo such as arm for linux/arm/v7) fails with an error.

An image that depends on another image (FROM __hive__/base:1.0 or a __hive__/ parent) can only be built for platforms that dependency configures. Building it for any other platform fails with an error naming the dependency and the platform. Add the platform to the dependency, or remove it from the dependent image.

docs.title: How multi-platform builds work
docs.text:
When you run ch build, ContainerHive builds each image once per platform. The output is a platform-specific OCI tar file:

dist/my-image/1.0.0/
├── linux-amd64/
│   └── image.tar
└── linux-arm64/
    └── image.tar

Each platform build runs independently through BuildKit, allowing parallel execution in CI.

docs.title: Creating multi-arch manifests with finalize
docs.text:
After building all platform-specific images, ch finalize creates OCI image indexes (multi-arch manifests) that reference all platform variants under a single tag:

ch finalize

This does two things:

  1. Creates manifests — For each image and tag, creates an OCI image index referencing all platform-specific images.
  2. Creates semantic version aliases — Generates shorter version tags that point to the full version manifest.

docs.title: Semantic version aliases
docs.text:
If your tags follow semantic versioning, finalize automatically creates alias tags pointing to the highest matching version:

Tag Generated aliases 1.2.3 1.2, 1 v2.0.1 v2.0, v2 1.2.3-alpine 1.2-alpine, 1-alpine 8.0.200 8.0, 8

When multiple tags compete for the same alias, the highest version wins. For example, if you build tags 1.2.3 and 1.3.0, the alias 1 points to 1.3.0.

docs.title: Supported version formats
docs.text:
• 1.2.3 — standard semver
  • v1.2.3 — with prefix (preserved in aliases)
  • 1.2.3.4 — four-component versions
  • 1.2.3-alpine — with suffix (preserved in aliases)

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
You can finalize specific images or tags:

ch finalize my-image:1.0.0

docs.title: Typical workflow
docs.text:
ch generate          # Render project configurations
ch build             # Build all platform-specific images
ch finalize          # Create multi-arch manifests and version aliases
ch test              # Run container structure tests
ch sbom              # Generate SBOMs

docs.title: CI pipeline integration
docs.text: Generated CI pipelines (via ch template ci) automatically handle multi-platform builds by creating separate build jobs per platform and a manifest job that runs finalize after all builds complete. See Generate CI pipelines.

docs.title: Build images with Nix flakes
docs.text:
[!WARNING] The Nix build backend is highly experimental. It is tested with small sample images only. Real projects may hit behaviors the samples do not cover. Try it, and file feedback at the issue tracker — any feedback is welcome.

Images in a ContainerHive project can define their filesystem with a Nix flake instead of a Dockerfile. ContainerHive resolves the project, builds the flake through BuildKit, and pushes, tests, and documents the result like any other image.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
ContainerHive runs nix build inside a Nix builder image through a custom BuildKit frontend:

  1. Discovery finds a flake.nix in the image directory and marks the image with the nix build backend.
  2. generate renders the image directory, copying flake.nix, flake.lock, the rootfs/ directory, and the test config into dist/.
  3. build executes a single executor step inside the configured builder image: nix build --option sandbox false in /src; the flake output is a rootfs directory, which becomes the image filesystem on an empty base.
  4. Everything else is unchanged: OCI labels, the S3 or registry build cache, multi-arch pushes, SBOMs, and structure tests run like on Dockerfile builds.

Only the BuildKit worker needs to pull the builder image. Neither ch nor the CI pipeline needs Nix installed.

The default builder image is the nix image of ContainerHive/helper-images, the official nixos/nix image with flakes enabled. That repository is itself a ContainerHive project and publishes one tag per Nix release series (2.35, 2.34, ...), so you can pin the Nix version your flakes need with a plain tag.

docs.title: The flake contract
docs.text:
The build produces a rootfs directory. The installed attribute is a convention, never user configured:

.#packages.<nix-system>.default

The <nix-system> maps from the target build platform, so the result does not depend on the system of the builder image. A flake must define that attribute for every platform it serves; nixpkgs.lib.systems.flakeExposed covers all systems at once:

{
  inputs.nixpkgs.url = "github:NixOS/nixpkgs";

  outputs = { self, nixpkgs }:
    {
      packages = nixpkgs.lib.genAttrs nixpkgs.lib.systems.flakeExposed (system:
        let
          pkgs = import nixpkgs { inherit system; };
        in
        {
          default = pkgs.buildEnv {
            name = "my-tool-rootfs";
            paths = [ pkgs.my-tool ];
          };
        });
    };
}

Platform mapping:

Docker platform Nix system linux/amd64 x86_64-linux linux/arm64 aarch64-linux linux/386 i686-linux linux/arm armv7l-linux linux/arm/v6 armv6l-linux linux/riscv64 riscv64-linux

Platforms without a mapping fail the build with a clear error. See the range of supported platforms for the project level view.

Keep the parent project files out of the flake. Static files the image should contain have to be part of the flake output. A rootfs/ directory next to the flake is not picked up automatically, and buildEnv only accepts derivations in paths, so wrap the directory in a derivation and add it to the buildEnv above:

let
  rootfs = pkgs.runCommand "my-tool-rootfs-files" { } "cp -r ${./rootfs} $out";
in
pkgs.buildEnv {
  name = "my-tool-rootfs";
  paths = [ pkgs.my-tool rootfs ];
}

docs.title: flake.lock handling
docs.text:
The lock file stays optional:

  • With flake.lock: the build respects it (--no-update-lock-file). When the flake input declarations no longer match the lock, the build fails with Nix's lock-file error instead of silently re-resolving. A flake.lock also stabilizes the BuildKit cache keys, so unchanged images build from cache on every machine that has them.
  • Without flake.lock: the build resolves inputs at build time (current HEAD of pinned github sources, deterministic store paths for pins). Discovery logs a warning. Builds are then not reproducible.

Commit a lock file for release workflows: run nix flake lock once and commit flake.lock next to flake.nix.

docs.title: Configure the backend in image.yml
docs.text:
Most images need no extra configuration:

description: "My tool image, built with Nix"
build: nix

tags:
  - name: 1.0.0

Set build: nix explicitly, or let discovery pick the backend: a flake.nix without a Dockerfile uses the Nix backend automatically. When both files exist, set build explicitly to remove the ambiguity.

The nix block configures the backend:

build: nix

nix:
  builder_image: "ghcr.io/containerhive/helper-images/nix:2.35"  # image providing the nix binary (default)
  extra_args: [ "--impure" ]       # extra nix build arguments

Because a flake has no Dockerfile instructions, the runtime configuration of the image looks like this:

config:
  entrypoint: [ "/bin/my-tool" ]
  cmd: [ "--help" ]
  env:
    TOOL_HOME: /var/lib/my-tool
  user: "1000:1000"
  working_dir: /workspace

Set working_dir, user, cmd, env, and entrypoint as needed. Unset fields stay empty.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text: Variants keep working: place a flake.nix into the variant directory and configure the variant like an image, with variant-level build, nix, and config blocks.

docs.title: Parent images
docs.text:
A flake build can start from a parent image rootfs instead of an empty base. Set nix.parent on the image or variant:

build: nix
depends_on:
  - base

nix:
  parent: "__hive__/base:1.0"

The value takes two forms:

  • __hive__/<name>:<tag> — another image of the project. ContainerHive resolves it from the local build cache like a Dockerfile dependency; CI resolves it from the registry. The build order derives from the reference; an explicit depends_on is not required.
  • __hive_parent__ — the variant placeholder. Only valid inside a variant: it resolves to the base tag __hive__/<name>:<tag> of the same image, so a variant of a flake image builds from that tag without more config.
  • Any other value is a plain image reference, for example ubuntu:22.04. It resolves through the registry and is digest-pinned like the builder image.

The build mounts the parent rootfs at /parent and copies it into the image first, so the flake output overlays the parent. Two limitations apply:

  • The flake cannot read the parent rootfs while it builds. Nix evaluates and builds in its own sandbox; the parent merge happens in the build script afterwards. Declare parent-provided file paths as image content, not as flake inputs.
  • The parent image config flows into the result (from semantics): entrypoint, cmd, env, user and working dir inherit from the parent unless the config block sets them. The env of the config block overlays the parent env per key.

docs.title: Build args and templating
docs.text:
A flake renders through the ContainerHive template engine like any other build entrypoint, so image versions and build args reach the flake through the template context. Name the templated flake flake.nix.gotpl; generate renders it and writes the result as flake.nix. A plain flake.nix is copied as is without template processing, so Nix would see the literal {{ ... }} expressions.

flake.nix.gotpl
{
  inputs.nixpkgs.url = "github:NixOS/nixpkgs?rev={{ .BuildArgs.nixpkgs_rev }}";

  outputs = { self, nixpkgs }: {
    packages = nixpkgs.lib.genAttrs nixpkgs.lib.systems.flakeExposed (system:
      let
        pkgs = import nixpkgs { inherit system; };
      in
      {
        default = pkgs.buildEnv { name = "my-tool-{{ .Versions.vm }}"; };
      });
  };
}

Two notes:

  • Rendering happens at generate time. A new build arg value re-renders the flake and invalidates the build cache, by design.
  • A rendered flake usually needs a committed flake.lock that stays stable against the rendered inputs; without one the build resolves freely (see the lock file section).

docs.title: Nix store caching
docs.text:
Every build otherwise starts with an empty nix store inside the builder container and re-downloads the closure of a changed flake. Set store_cache: true to keep the store across builds:

build: nix

nix:
  store_cache: true

The script imports the build closure from a persistent BuildKit cache mount before the build and saves the new closure after it. A changed flake reuses the downloaded packages instead of re-fetching them. Three limits apply:

  • The cache mount lives inside one BuildKit daemon. A fresh daemon starts cold.
  • The registry or S3 build cache does not carry the store. For cross-machine warmup, pin the flake inputs with flake.lock and let nix substitute from a binary cache.
  • The saves are best effort and grow unbounded across builds of the daemon. Clear the cache mount when it grows too large.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Multi-platform nix build runs under emulation on non-native machines. Expect slow first builds for arm64 on x86 builders; BuildKit caches the step afterwards. The build runs with filter-syscalls = false because Nix syscall filtering does not work under emulation, a known limitation. Understood trade-off when you accept the nix backend.
  • The flake cannot read the parent rootfs while it builds (see parent images).

docs.title: Pre-commit integration
docs.text: ContainerHive ships pre-commit hooks that let you automate CI pipeline generation, project verification, and other ContainerHive commands directly in your development workflow.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add the ContainerHive hook repository to your .pre-commit-config.yaml:

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/ContainerHive/pre-commit
    rev: main # use tag or commit hash for your projects
    hooks:
      - id: template
      - id: verify

docs.title: run
docs.text:
Run an arbitrary ContainerHive command. By default runs ch with no subcommand. Pass arguments via args.

- id: run
  args: [ generate ]

docs.title: Example: automated CI pipeline generation
docs.text:
The following example can be used to keep CI pipelines in sync with the project definition:

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/ContainerHive/pre-commit
    rev: main # use tag or commit hash for your projects
    hooks:
      - id: template
        args:
          - ci
          - --provider
          - github
          - --output
          - .github/workflows/main.yml

Every time hive.yml or any image.yml changes, pre-commit re-generates the GitHub Actions workflow so it always reflects the current project state.

docs.title: Clean up registry images with retention policies
docs.text: Every pipeline run — including merge request (MR) and pull request (PR) pipelines — pushes images to the configured registry. Without cleanup, these images accumulate indefinitely. This page explains what gets pushed and how to set up retention policies to keep your registry tidy.

docs.title: Why images accumulate
docs.text:
ContainerHive pushes images on every CI run because downstream steps depend on them:

  1. ch build pushes per-platform intermediate images so ch test can pull them back for validation.
  2. ch finalize creates multi-arch manifests and pushes semantic version aliases.
  3. With --build-id, all tags are suffixed with -build.<id> (e.g. 1.0.0-build.mr-42), so each MR/PR run leaves permanent, distinct tags behind — even if the MR is never merged.

Because skipping these pushes would break the test and finalize steps, the recommended approach is to configure retention policies on the registry itself to automatically clean up images after a suitable grace period.

docs.title: What gets pushed
docs.text:
Image kind Example tag When pushed Retention target Per-platform intermediates 1.0.0.linux-amd64 Every run (overwritten per tag) Overwrite-safe; accumulate only with --build-id Build-ID intermediates 1.0.0.linux-amd64-build.mr-42 MR/PR runs with --build-id Short-lived (days) Build-ID manifests 1.0.0-build.mr-42 MR/PR runs with --build-id Short-lived (days) Build-ID aliases 1-build.mr-42 MR/PR runs with --build-id Short-lived (days) Default branch tags 1.0.0, 1.0, 1 Main/default branch only Keep (long-lived) Registry cache layers Under cache.ref repository Every run Medium-lived (weeks)

To target snapshot images for cleanup without touching production tags, match tags containing -build. as the infix — for example *-build.* — or filter by image name pattern.

docs.title: Recommended retention windows
docs.text: Category Retention Rationale Snapshot images (-build.*) A few days MRs are typically reviewed and merged (or closed) within days Cache layers A few weeks Older cache layers have diminishing hit rates and waste storage Default branch tags Keep indefinitely These are your production releases

docs.title: GitLab Container Registry
docs.text:
GitLab has a built-in cleanup policy per repository. It runs on a schedule (daily or weekly) and can remove tags matching a name pattern.

Recommended configuration:

  1. Navigate to Settings > Packages and registries > Container Registry in your project.
  2. Enable Cleanup policy.
  3. Set Keep tags matching: ^[0-9].* (keeps version tags like 1.0.0, 1.2.3).
  4. Set Remove tags matching: .*-build\..* (removes all build-ID suffixed tags).
  5. Set Expiration: 3 days for .*-build\..* tags, keep version tags indefinitely.
  6. Schedule: weekly is sufficient for most projects.

Alternatively, use the GitLab API in a scheduled CI job:

cleanup:
  stage: cleanup
  image: curlimages/curl
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      when: always
  script:
    - |
      curl --request DELETE \
        --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_CLEANUP_TOKEN" \
        "https://gitlab.com/api/v4/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/\
          container_repository?tag_name_regex=.*-build\..*&expire_in=3d"
  allow_failure: true

Protected and shared tags

GitLab's cleanup policy skips tags marked as protected or shared. Ensure your MR build-ID tags are not accidentally protected — this is rarely an issue since build-ID tags are transient.

docs.title: GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io)
docs.text:
GitHub does not provide a built-in retention policy for the Container Registry. Use the container-retention-policy action in a scheduled workflow:

name: Cleanup container images

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 0 * * 0"  # weekly on Sunday

jobs:
  cleanup:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      packages: write
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Delete old snapshot images
        uses: snok/container-retention-policy@v3
        with:
          image-name: ".*"
          tag-pattern: ".*-build\\..*"
          cut-off: "3d"
          keep-at-least: 0
          skip-tags: "latest,^[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+$"
          account-type: "org"
          org-name: "your-org"
          token: ${{ secrets.DELETE_PACKAGES_TOKEN }}

Setup steps:

  1. Create a personal access token (classic) with the delete:packages scope — or a fine-grained token with packages: write on the target org.
  2. Store it as a repository secret named DELETE_PACKAGES_TOKEN.
  3. Add the workflow above to .github/workflows/cleanup.yml and adjust org-name and image-name as needed.

Permissions required

The built-in GITHUB_TOKEN does not have permission to delete packages. A PAT or a fine-grained token with packages: write is required. The org-name field is only needed for organization-owned registries — remove it for user accounts.

docs.title: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR)
docs.text:
ECR supports lifecycle policies that automatically expire images. Create a lifecycle policy JSON file matching the repository:

{
  "rules": [
    {
      "rulePriority": 1,
      "description": "Expire build-ID snapshot images after 3 days",
      "selection": {
        "tagStatus": "tagged",
        "tagPatternList": [
          "*-build.*"
        ],
        "repositoryName": "your-repo",
        "countType": "sinceImagePushed",
        "countUnit": "days",
        "countNumber": 3
      },
      "action": {
        "type": "expire"
      }
    },
    {
      "rulePriority": 2,
      "description": "Keep at most 100 untagged images",
      "selection": {
        "tagStatus": "untagged",
        "repositoryName": "your-repo",
        "countType": "imageCountMoreThan",
        "countNumber": 100
      },
      "action": {
        "type": "expire"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Apply it with the AWS CLI:

aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy \
  --repository-name your-repo \
  --lifecycle-policy-text file://lifecycle-policy.json

Apply to all repositories

Omit repositoryName from the selection to apply the rule across all repositories in the registry.

docs.title: Harbor
docs.text:
Harbor supports tag retention rules at the project level.

  1. Navigate to your project in the Harbor UI.
  2. Go to Interrogation Services > Tag Retention Rules.
  3. Create a new rule:
    • Repository matching: **/* (all repositories in the project)
    • Tag matching: .*-build\..*
    • Retention: 3 days
    • Most recently pushed: N/A (use age-based)
  4. Add a second rule for cache images:
    • Repository matching: the cache repository (e.g. cache/*)
    • Tag matching: **
    • Retention: 3 weeks

You can also define retention rules via the Harbor API: POST /api/v2.0/retentions.

docs.title: Docker Hub
docs.text:
Docker Hub does not provide built-in retention policies. For automated cleanup, use scheduled jobs with the Docker Hub API: delete tags matching your snapshot pattern on a schedule.

# Delete a specific tag
curl -X DELETE \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DOCKER_HUB_TOKEN" \
  "https://hub.docker.com/v2/repositories/your-org/your-repo/tags/1.0.0-build.mr-42"

For a ready-made solution, consider the docker-hub-delete-tags action or similar community tools that support regex-based tag deletion.

Rate limits

Docker Hub API rate limits apply. For projects with many tags, batch deletions and space your API calls to avoid hitting limits.

docs.title: Generic OCI registries
docs.text:
For self-hosted OCI registries (zot, Distribution, Quay, JFrog Artifactory, etc.), use the registry's own tag management API or a scheduled job that iterates tags and deletes those matching your snapshot pattern.

If you use BuildKit with a registry cache backend (configured via cache.ref in hive.yml), the cache repository will also grow over time. Set up a separate, longer-lived retention policy (e.g. 3 weeks) on the cache repository to keep recent layers while discarding stale ones.

docs.title: Renovate integration
docs.text: ContainerHive ships a Renovate preset that enables automated version bump PRs for the versions: entries in your image.yml files. It uses the regex manager together with inline comments to identify which values to track and how.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add the preset to your renovate.json5:

{
  "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  "extends": [
    // your other presets ...
    "github>ContainerHive/ContainerHive//renovate/image-versions.json5"
  ]
}

docs.title: Annotating versions
docs.text:
Add a # renovate: comment to any version entry you want Renovate to track:

versions:
  python: "3.13.7"    # renovate: datasource=pypi depName=python versioning=pep440
  zig: "0.14.1"       # renovate: datasource=github-releases depName=ziglang/zig
  nodejs: "24"        # renovate: datasource=node depName=node versioning=node

Annotations work at all three version levels — image, tag, and variant:

versions:
  uv: "0.8.22" # renovate: datasource=pypi depName=uv versioning=pep440

tags:
  - name: "3.13.7"
    versions:
      python: "3.13.7" # renovate: datasource=pypi depName=python versioning=pep440

variants:
  - name: slim
    tag_suffix: -slim
    versions:
      python: "3.13.7-slim" # renovate: datasource=docker depName=python versioning=docker

docs.title: Comment fields
docs.text: Field Required Description datasource= yes Renovate datasource — e.g. pypi, docker, github-releases, go, node depName= yes Package or image name as the datasource knows it versioning= no Versioning scheme (default: semver) — e.g. pep440, docker, node registryUrl= no Custom registry URL for private registries

docs.text:
PyPIDocker HubGitHub ReleasesGoNode.jsPrivate registry

  python: "3.13.7"  # renovate: datasource=pypi depName=python versioning=pep440
  uv: "0.8.22"      # renovate: datasource=pypi depName=uv versioning=pep440

versions:
  ubuntu: "24.04" # renovate: datasource=docker depName=ubuntu versioning=docker

versions:
  zig: "0.14.1"   # renovate: datasource=github-releases depName=ziglang/zig
  kubectl: "1.32.0" # renovate: datasource=github-releases depName=kubernetes/kubernetes versioning=semver

  golang: "1.23.0" # renovate: datasource=go depName=go versioning=semver

docs.title: Manage versions and secrets
docs.text: ContainerHive provides a structured way to manage versions and secrets across your image definitions, with a clear merge hierarchy and multiple secret backends.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: Versions are key-value pairs that flow through your entire build pipeline — from image.yml through Dockerfiles and test definitions.

docs.title: Defining versions
docs.text:
Versions can be set at three levels, with each level overriding the previous:

1. Image level (defaults for all tags):

# image.yml
versions:
  python: "3.13"
  uv: "0.8.22"

2. Tag level (overrides per tag):

tags:
  - name: 3.13.7
    versions:
      python: "3.13.7"    # overrides image-level "3.13"
                           # uv remains "0.8.22"
  - name: 3.12.9
    versions:
      python: "3.12.9"

3. Variant level (overrides per variant):

variants:
  - name: slim
    tag_suffix: -slim
    versions:
      python: "3.13.7-slim"   # overrides tag-level value

docs.title: Using versions in Dockerfiles
docs.text:
Versions are automatically converted to Docker build arguments with an uppercase _VERSION suffix. Hyphens are replaced with underscores.

Version key Docker ARG python PYTHON_VERSION dotnet-sdk-channel DOTNET_SDK_CHANNEL_VERSION nodejs NODEJS_VERSION 
ARG PYTHON_VERSION
FROM python:${PYTHON_VERSION}

docs.title: Using versions in templates
docs.text:
In .gotpl files (Dockerfiles or tests), versions are also available as template variables:

FROM python:{{ .Versions.python }}

docs.title: Using versions in test definitions
docs.text:
In test.yml.gotpl:

schemaVersion: 2.0.0
commandTests:
  - name: "Python version"
    command: "python"
    args: ["--version"]
    expectedOutput: ["Python {{ .Versions.python }}"]

docs.title: Build arguments
docs.text:
Build arguments work the same as versions but without the _VERSION suffix transformation.

# image.yml
build_args:
  foo: bar

tags:
  - name: latest
    build_args:
      foo: baz     # overrides image-level value for this tag

ARG foo
RUN echo "${foo}"

In .gotpl templates: {{ .BuildArgs.foo }}.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: Secrets are mounted into the build process via BuildKit's secret mount mechanism. They are never baked into image layers.

docs.title: Defining secrets
docs.text:
# image.yml
secrets:
  my_credentials:
    source: env
    value: API_KEY

docs.title: Secret sources
docs.text: Source Description Example env Read from an environment variable value: API_KEY or value: ${API_KEY} plain Use the value as-is value: my-secret-token vault Fetch from HashiCorp Vault value: vault://secret/data/app#token

docs.title: Using secrets in Dockerfiles
docs.text:
Mount secrets with BuildKit's --mount=type=secret syntax:

RUN --mount=type=secret,id=my_credentials \
    cat /run/secrets/my_credentials

The id must match the key name from your image.yml secrets definition.

docs.title: Environment variable resolution
docs.text: The env source supports both $VAR and ${VAR} syntax. The value is resolved at build time from the environment where ch build runs.

docs.title: Vault integration
docs.text:
For Vault secrets, set VAULT_ADDR to your Vault instance URL and provide authentication via VAULT_TOKEN or ~/.vault-token:

secrets:
  db_password:
    source: vault
    value: vault://secret/data/myapp#db_password

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
# image.yml
versions:
  dotnet-sdk-channel: "8.0"
  nodejs: "24"

build_args:
  extra_packages: "curl git"

secrets:
  registry_token:
    source: env
    value: REGISTRY_TOKEN

tags:
  - name: 8.0.100
    versions:
      dotnet-sdk-channel: "8.0.1xx"
  - name: 8.0.200
    versions:
      dotnet-sdk-channel: "8.0.2xx"

variants:
  - name: node
    tag_suffix: -node
    versions:
      nodejs: "24"

FROM ubuntu:24.04

ARG DOTNET_SDK_CHANNEL_VERSION
ARG extra_packages
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y ${extra_packages}
RUN install-dotnet --channel "${DOTNET_SDK_CHANNEL_VERSION}"

RUN --mount=type=secret,id=registry_token \
    configure-registry /run/secrets/registry_token

docs.title: Split work across shards
docs.text:
ch build, ch sbom and ch test can split the images and tags they process across a fixed number of CI jobs, so a large project can build, generate SBOMs, and test in parallel instead of one long serial job.

Generated CI also creates a separate test job for each configured platform. ci_test_shards applies to each platform job, so test parallelism scales with both the number of platforms and the configured shard count. Each job tests only its platform; GitHub Actions uses a matching native runner, while GitLab jobs extend .test-<arch> bases that can be assigned architecture-specific runner tags.

The main motivation is GitLab.com's SaaS limits on SBOM report artifacts: 10 MB per file, 20 MB per job. A single build job today uploads the CycloneDX SBOM of every tag and variant of an image, so an image with many tags or variants can push the job over that budget — and the job is also slower because all of that work runs serially. Splitting one job into several parallel: instances, each owning a disjoint slice of the tags, keeps every job under the artifact ceiling and cuts wall-clock time on variant-heavy images.

docs.title: Shard unit
docs.text:
Every base tag and every variant tag is its own shard unit, addressed by the image and the exact tag name. This is deliberately fine-grained: an image with 20 variants of one base tag needs to split at the variant level, not the base-tag level, or a single job would still hold all 20 SBOMs.

One rule follows from this: a variant's Dockerfile is FROM its own base tag (e.g. dotnet:8.0.200-node is FROM __hive__/dotnet:8.0.200), and that dependency is invisible to ContainerHive's dependency graph because it's a same-image reference. So a shard that owns a variant also builds that variant's base tag, even if the base isn't assigned to it by exact match. The base may therefore be built redundantly by more than one shard — cheap, since BuildKit caches it and the resulting push is content-identical — while ch sbom and ch test still gate on exact tag ownership, so SBOM output stays strictly disjoint across shards. That disjointness is what the per-job artifact budget depends on.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Description --max-shards Total number of shards to split work across — sourced from CI_NODE_TOTAL env (default: 1) --current-shard This shard's 1-based index — sourced from CI_NODE_INDEX env (default: 1)

--max-shards/--current-shard and CI_NODE_TOTAL/CI_NODE_INDEX behave as flag over env over default. GitLab sets CI_NODE_TOTAL/CI_NODE_INDEX automatically for a job declared with parallel: N, so sharding works with no flags at all under parallel:. The variable names are vendor-neutral by design — a CI provider without native parallel-job fan-out can export the same two variables from a wrapper script and get the same behavior.

docs.title: GitLab template options
docs.text:
The generated GitLab pipeline exposes two template options to control shard count without hand-editing the pipeline:

Option Description ci_build_shards Upper bound on parallel instances for each build job (default: 1). Capped per image to the number of shard units the image actually has. ci_test_shards Upper bound on parallel instances for each platform-specific test job (default: 1). Capped per image to the number of shard units the image actually has. 
# hive.yml
template_options:
  ci_build_shards: "5"

At the default of 1, the rendered pipeline has no parallel: key at all — not parallel: 1, which is meaningless and renames the job to ... 1/1. Regenerate the pipeline after changing either option:

ch template ci --provider gitlab --output .gitlab-ci.yml --image-name <your-image>

docs.title: Build and SBOM must run in the same job
docs.text: ch sbom only reads local dist/<image>/<tag>/<platform>/image.tar — it never pulls from a registry, deliberately, since pulling a full image just to produce a comparatively small SBOM is the cost sharding exists to avoid. This means a shard's ch build and ch sbom must run in the same CI job, so the tars ch sbom needs are already on disk. The generated GitLab pipeline already does this (ch build followed by ch sbom in the same .build job template), so setting ci_build_shards is sufficient — no extra wiring needed. If you assemble a pipeline by hand, keep this pairing.

docs.title: Cross-image dependencies
docs.text: A project with __hive__/ references between different images (not the same-image base/variant case above) needs the dependency image fully built and pushed before a dependent shard starts, since a missing local tar falls back to a registry pull. The generated GitLab pipeline already stages this correctly — each build job depends on the manifest-<image> job of its dependencies — so this is only a concern for hand-rolled pipelines. Enabling sharding on a project with such dependencies logs a warning rather than failing, since the registry fallback is a legitimate (if slower) path.

docs.title: Zero-unit shards
docs.text:
More shards than units is a normal, supported configuration — for example ci_build_shards: 10 on a project with a single image. When using the generated GitLab pipeline, ci_build_shards / ci_test_shards are capped per image to the number of shard units that image has, so over-provisioned shards only arise in hand-rolled pipelines.

In a hand-rolled pipeline (or any pipeline setting CI_NODE_TOTAL directly), assignment is modulo round-robin over a canonically sorted unit list, so a single unit always lands in shard 1 and shards 2 through 10 simply own nothing. A shard that owns nothing logs "Nothing to do for this shard" and exits 0, so an over-provisioned shard count never fails the pipeline.

docs.title: Cross-command alignment
docs.text: ch build, ch sbom and ch test compute the same canonical, sorted list of shard units from the project, so shard N of M always selects the same tags in every command — ch build --max-shards 3 --current-shard 2 and ch sbom --max-shards 3 --current-shard 2 operate on the same slice.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Sharding addresses the 20 MB per-job artifact limit by splitting work across jobs. It does not help with the 10 MB per-file limit — a single cyclonedx.json for one tag on one platform that is itself larger than 10 MB is not made smaller by adding more shards, since the shard unit is one tag, not a fraction of one SBOM.

ch finalize is never sharded. It runs once, after all shards have completed, and needs the project's complete tag set to resolve multi-arch manifests and semantic version aliases correctly.

See Filter images and tags for image:tag filters, which compose with sharding: filters select which images and tags are in scope at all, and sharding partitions whatever remains after filtering.

docs.title: Test your containers
docs.text: ContainerHive integrates container-structure-test by Google to validate built images as part of the build process.

docs.title: Writing test definitions
docs.text:
Test definitions are written as Go templates (test.yml.gotpl) placed alongside the Dockerfile in the image directory.

images/my-image/
├── image.yml
├── Dockerfile
└── test.yml.gotpl

The template is rendered with the image context (versions, build args, etc.) during ch generate, producing the final test YAML in dist/.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
schemaVersion: "2.0.0"

fileExistenceTests:
  - name: "Check binary exists"
    path: "/usr/local/bin/my-app"
    shouldExist: true
    permissions: "-rwxr-xr-x"

commandTests:
  - name: "Check version output"
    command: "my-app"
    args: ["--version"]
    expectedOutput: ["{{ .Versions.app }}"]

fileContentTests:
  - name: "Check config file"
    path: "/etc/my-app/config.yml"
    expectedContents: ["production"]

Since the test file is a Go template, you can reference versions and build args from your image.yml:

commandTests:
  - name: "Python version"
    command: "python3"
    args: ["--version"]
    expectedOutput: ["Python {{ .Versions.python }}"]

docs.title: Variant tests
docs.text:
Variants can have their own test definitions by placing a test.yml.gotpl in the variant subdirectory:

images/my-image/
├── image.yml
├── Dockerfile
├── test.yml.gotpl
└── slim/
    ├── Dockerfile
    └── test.yml.gotpl

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
After building images, run tests with:

ch test

This will:

  1. Collect rendered test definitions from dist/<image>/<tag>/tests/.
  2. Load or pull the built image for each platform.
  3. Execute the tests and produce JUnit XML reports.

docs.title: Building before tests
docs.text:
Use --build to build images first, then run tests:

ch test --build

You can combine with --generate to render templates, build, and test in one step:

ch test --generate --build

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
You can run tests for specific images or tags:

ch test my-image:latest
ch test my-image:*

When using --build, the same filters apply to both the build and test steps.

docs.title: CI behavior
docs.text: In CI environments (CI env var is set), ContainerHive automatically starts a local registry and falls back to pulling images from it when no local tar file is found.

docs.title: Test reports
docs.text:
JUnit XML reports are written to the platform directory under dist/:

dist/my-image/latest/linux-amd64/my-image-latest-cst-report.xml

These reports can be consumed by CI systems for test result visualization.
